critic.title: Revelation 1-7: An Exegetical Commentary

critic.author: Grant R. Osborne
critic.title: Revelation (Baker Exegetical Commentary on the New Testament)

sequence: Christ's victory at the cross and ascension
Satan cast down and restrained
Church as faithful witness in the wilderness
Cycle: seals, trumpets and bowls of judgment recur
Beasts and Babylon rise in each era
Martyrs vindicated and reigning with Christ
Final climactic opposition
Christ returns; last judgment
New Jerusalem: God dwells with his people

readings.reading: A future, literal binding of Satan after Christ's visible return (Rev 19), removing his influence from the earth so that Christ's reign from Jerusalem proceeds without deception. The sequence of chapters 19 and 20 is chronological.

Satan is bound after the second coming described in Rev 19:11-21, so the millennium follows the return. The thousand years may or may not be exactly literal, but the binding is a future event that ends Satan's deception of the nations.

The binding happened through Christ's first coming, as when Jesus binds the strong man (Matt 12:29) and casts out the ruler of this world (John 12:31). Satan is restrained specifically from deceiving the nations so that the gospel goes to all peoples.

Satan's binding began with Christ's victory and is progressively displayed as the gospel conquers the nations. The thousand years is a long era, ultimately a golden age of gospel success, before a brief final apostasy.

Most partial preterists read Rev 20 within an amillennial or postmillennial frame: the binding is tied to Christ's first-century victory, while the vision of the final loosing and judgment remains future. Interpreters differ on which frame fits best.

The binding and the thousand years belong to the transitional period between Christ's ministry and AD 70 (often read as a symbolic span of roughly forty years). The loosing and final battle are tied to the Jewish War and the fall of Jerusalem.

A symbolic picture of Christ's decisive victory over Satan at the cross, restraining evil's power to deceive the nations throughout the church age. Revelation 20 recapitulates the whole age rather than following chapter 19 in time.

The first resurrection is a bodily resurrection of tribulation martyrs (with the church already raised at the rapture), who reign on earth with Christ for a literal thousand years. The rest of the dead are raised at the end.

The same Greek verb (ezesan, they came to life) describes both the first resurrection and the rest of the dead, so both are bodily resurrections separated by the millennium. Believers reign with Christ on earth between them.

The thrones are in heaven, where the souls of departed believers reign with Christ during the present age. The first resurrection is either regeneration or the believer's entrance into heavenly life at death; the second death has no power over them.

The reign of the saints is the triumph of Christ's cause on earth, sometimes read as the revival of the martyrs' cause in later generations. Warfield read it as the blessedness of the saints in heaven during the age; others stress gospel dominion.

The martyrs in view are first-century witnesses killed under Rome and Jerusalem's persecution, now vindicated and reigning with Christ. Their reign spans the church age, which continues until Christ's future bodily return.
The first resurrection is a spiritual coming-to-life of the faithful during the apostolic generation; the reign was fulfilled as the covenant transition concluded in AD 70.

A heavenly-throne vision assuring persecuted believers in every era that those who die faithful are not defeated but reign with Christ. The scene answers the question of the souls under the altar in Rev 6:9-11.

Sixty-nine weeks of years run to the Messiah; a gap (the church age) follows; the seventieth week is a future seven-year tribulation that begins when a coming prince makes a covenant with Israel and breaks it midway.

Views vary. Many historic premillennialists accept that the final week is at least partly eschatological, but they do not require a pretribulation removal of the church or a strict Israel-church division.

The seventy weeks run continuously to Christ. He confirms the covenant, his death ends sacrifice in principle in the middle of the week, and the desolation points to the destruction of Jerusalem. No gap is required.

Read as fulfilled in Christ's first coming and the events of the first century: Messiah is cut off, the new covenant confirmed, and the temple later destroyed. This frees the future for gospel advance rather than a coming tribulation.

Fulfilled in the first century: Christ's ministry and death, then the Roman destruction of the city and temple in AD 70, which Jesus himself connected to Daniel's abomination of desolation (Matt 24:15).
Entirely fulfilled by AD 70, including the bringing in of everlasting righteousness and the sealing of vision and prophecy, which are read as the completion of all prophecy at that point.
Idealists often follow a messianic, first-century reading of Daniel while stressing its typological pattern: tyrants who desecrate God's worship recur, and Christ's sacrifice is the decisive center.
Describes the visible return of Christ at the end of the future tribulation. This generation refers to the generation alive when these signs begin, or to the Jewish race, not to Jesus' hearers.
Jesus blends the near judgment on Jerusalem with the final coming of the Son of Man; the gathering of the elect after the tribulation is the church's rapture at a single posttribulational return.

Many amillennialists see a double reference: verses up to the fall of Jerusalem were fulfilled in AD 70, while the coming in glory foreshadowed there is the one future return. Others split the discourse at verse 36.
Most modern postmillennialists read verses 4-34 as fulfilled in AD 70, with the cosmic imagery borrowed from prophetic judgment oracles (Isa 13:10), and verses 36 onward as the future second coming.

Everything through verse 34 happened within Jesus' generation: the coming on the clouds is Christ's coming in judgment on Jerusalem, echoing Dan 7:13. A future bodily return is taught in passages such as Acts 1:11 and 1 Cor 15.
The whole discourse, including Christ's coming and the gathering of the elect, was fulfilled within that generation; there is no reason to postpone any part of it.
The discourse gives a pattern of tribulation, false messiahs and judgment that is first realized in AD 70 and repeatedly echoed until the final coming of Christ.
After the fullness of the Gentiles (the church age), national Israel will be saved at Christ's return and enjoy the land and kingdom promises in the millennium.
Anticipates a future large-scale turning of ethnic Israel to Christ, probably connected with the second coming, while Jews and Gentiles share one people of God.

Many amillennialists read all Israel as the total of elect Jews across history or as the whole people of God; others accept a future ingathering of Jews into the one church without a millennial kingdom.
A future mass conversion of ethnic Jews will help bring in worldwide gospel blessing, as Puritan and Princeton postmillennialists expected (life from the dead, Rom 11:15).
Partial preterists follow their amillennial or postmillennial frame here; many postmillennial preterists expect a future conversion of Jews within the church age.
Often read as fulfilled in the first-century gathering of a believing remnant of Israel into the new covenant community before AD 70.
Read within the redemptive-historical frame of one people of God; idealists differ on whether a future ingathering of Jews is in view.
Because death still occurs (verse 20), this describes the millennial kingdom on the present earth, a stage before the final eternal state.
An intermediate kingdom is suggested where long life, building and planting continue but death is not yet abolished, fitting an earthly millennium.
Prophetic poetry describing the new creation in the idioms of Israel's life; long life and the absence of infant death express fullness of blessing, fulfilled in Rev 21:1-4.
Depicts the gradual transformation of the world by the gospel within history, a golden age before final consummation.
The new creation was inaugurated in Christ and the new covenant (2 Cor 5:17); its fullness awaits the future return, so the passage has already and not-yet aspects.
The new heavens and new earth are the new covenant order that fully replaced the old covenant world in AD 70.
A symbolic portrait of God's renewed world which John takes up in Rev 21-22, describing the final state in images drawn from Israel's hopes.
Jesus does not deny that the kingdom will be restored to Israel, only that the timing is not theirs to know; the visible ascension promises a visible return to the Mount of Olives (Zech 14:4).
The kingdom restoration remains a future hope linked to Christ's visible bodily return in the same way he departed.
Jesus redirects the disciples from a national restoration to a Spirit-empowered worldwide witness. The return is personal, visible and single.
The Spirit-empowered mission to the ends of the earth is the means by which Christ's kingdom will fill the world before his visible return.
This is the key text for a future bodily return: the angels say he will come in the same way, bodily and visibly, which AD 70 did not fulfil.
The same way is read as coming in a cloud of glory and judgment, which full preterists believe was fulfilled in AD 70, perceived spiritually rather than physically.
The ascension frames the church age as the time of witness; the promised return is the final consummation toward which Revelation's cycles move.
The man of lawlessness is a future antichrist revealed after the restrainer, often identified with the Holy Spirit's work through the church, is removed at the rapture.
The church will see the apostasy and the man of lawlessness before the Lord's coming and our gathering to him, which supports a posttribulational return.
A final personal antichrist is expected just before the one return, while the mystery of lawlessness is already at work throughout the age.
Many postmillennialists place the man of lawlessness in the first century (some suggest a Jewish or Roman figure) or in a brief final apostasy after the golden age.
Often identified with a first-century figure, such as Nero or the leadership of the Jewish revolt, destroyed in the judgment of AD 70.
Entirely first-century: the man of lawlessness, the restrainer and the Lord's coming all belong to the period before AD 70.
Describes the recurring spirit of lawless opposition to God that will culminate in a final manifestation before Christ's return.

timeline.title: Papias of Hierapolis
timeline.note: Teaches an earthly kingdom after the resurrection, according to fragments preserved by Irenaeus and Eusebius. Eusebius judged him to have misunderstood apostolic accounts.

timeline.title: Justin Martyr's Dialogue with Trypho
timeline.note: Justin expects a thousand-year reign in a rebuilt Jerusalem, while acknowledging that some orthodox Christians think otherwise (chapters 80-81).

timeline.title: Irenaeus, Against Heresies Book 5
timeline.note: Chapters 32-36 defend a literal earthly kingdom of the righteous as part of his argument against Gnostic denial of the goodness of creation.

timeline.title: Dionysius of Alexandria answers Nepos
timeline.note: Dionysius debates the millenarian teaching of Bishop Nepos in Egypt, according to Eusebius, Church History 7.24-25. Alexandrian exegesis increasingly reads the kingdom spiritually.

timeline.title: Tyconius' rules of interpretation
timeline.note: The Donatist scholar Tyconius reads Revelation as describing the church's whole history, a reading that shapes Augustine.

timeline.title: Augustine completes City of God
timeline.note: Book 20 reads the thousand years as the present church age and the first resurrection as spiritual. This becomes the dominant Western view for over a millennium.

timeline.title: Augsburg Confession, Article 17
timeline.note: Lutherans reject teaching that the godly will possess a worldly kingdom before the resurrection of the dead. The Second Helvetic Confession (1566) issues a similar rejection.

timeline.title: Luis de Alcazar's preterist commentary
timeline.note: The Jesuit scholar publishes a commentary reading most of Revelation as fulfilled in the early centuries, a landmark for preterist interpretation.

timeline.title: Daniel Whitby and the rise of postmillennialism
timeline.note: Whitby's treatise on the millennium, building on Puritan hopes for gospel success, popularizes a future golden age before Christ's return.

timeline.title: Jonathan Edwards preaches the History of Redemption
timeline.note: Edwards' sermon series (published 1774) sets out a hopeful vision of worldwide gospel triumph before the end.

timeline.title: Darby develops dispensationalism
timeline.note: In the late 1820s and 1830s John Nelson Darby and the Brethren develop a sharp distinction between Israel and the church and a pretribulation rapture. Exact dates are debated.

timeline.title: J. Stuart Russell's The Parousia
timeline.note: Russell argues that all of Christ's coming, including resurrection and judgment, occurred by AD 70, the seed of later full preterism.

timeline.title: Scofield Reference Bible
timeline.note: C. I. Scofield's notes spread dispensational premillennialism across English-speaking evangelicalism.

timeline.title: The Meaning of the Millennium: Four Views
timeline.note: Robert Clouse edits a landmark exchange in which Ladd, Hoyt, Boettner and Hoekema present and critique each view.

timeline.title: G. K. Beale's Revelation commentary
timeline.note: Beale's eclectic idealist commentary (NIGTC) presents a major scholarly case for reading Revelation symbolically with an amillennial view of chapter 20.

influence.note: Dispensationalism inherited the expectation of an earthly reign after the return, adding the Israel-church distinction and a pretribulation rapture.
Tyconius' symbolic, church-age reading of Revelation fed directly into Augustine's amillennial interpretation.
Augustine's present-reign reading was adapted by Puritans and later Reformed theologians into an optimistic expectation of gospel triumph.
Modern postmillennialists such as Gentry and Mathison have championed partial preterism as the exegetical foundation for their optimism.
Full preterism extends the partial preterist reading of the time texts to every coming, resurrection and judgment passage.
Modern eclectic idealism (Hendriksen, Beale) typically adopts an amillennial reading of Rev 20.

argumentMap.text: Christ returns before an earthly thousand-year kingdom, which follows the sequence of Rev 19-20.
The same verb describes both resurrections in Rev 20:4-5, implying two bodily resurrections a thousand years apart.
Elsewhere the resurrection of righteous and wicked is presented as a single hour or day.
Prophetic hour language can span an extended period, as the hour of John 5:25 already spans the church age.
God's promises to national Israel require a literal future kingdom distinct from the church.
Consistent literal interpretation of unconditional covenants requires a land fulfillment not yet seen.
The New Testament applies Israel's promises to the multiethnic church in Christ, the true seed of Abraham.
Inclusion of Gentiles does not cancel promises to ethnic Israel; Paul still speaks of Israel's future.
The thousand years symbolizes the present age in which Satan is bound and the saints reign with Christ.
Jesus already describes binding the strong man and casting out Satan through his ministry and cross.
Satan is described as active and deceptive in the present age, which does not look like being sealed in an abyss.
The binding is specific: he cannot prevent the nations from hearing the gospel, while other activity continues.
The gospel will progressively win the great majority of the world before Christ returns.
Christ reigns now until all enemies are put under his feet, and the kingdom grows like leaven.
Jesus and Paul anticipate apostasy, persecution and lawlessness up to the end.
Many such texts describe the first century or a brief final apostasy, not the whole age.
Jesus' time statements locate the Olivet tribulation and coming in judgment within his own generation.
If the time texts must be applied to AD 70, consistency demands applying all coming texts there too.
Not every coming text has a time marker; the bodily return of Acts 1:11 and the resurrection of 1 Cor 15 remain future.
Full preterism contradicts the historic creeds' confession of a future return, bodily resurrection and judgment.
Revelation portrays timeless principles of the conflict between Christ and evil, recapitulated in parallel cycles.
John addresses seven real churches about things that must soon take place, implying concrete historical reference.
Eclectic idealism affirms the first-century setting and a future consummation while reading the symbols as applying to every era.

title: The Rapture and the Return of Christ
question: When is the church gathered to Christ?
intro:
Paul tells the Thessalonians that when the Lord descends from heaven, the dead in Christ will rise first and living believers will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air (1 Thess 4:16-17). The Latin Vulgate's verb for caught up, rapiemur, gives the English word rapture. That believers will be gathered to Christ at his coming is stated in the text; the debated question is when this gathering happens relative to a final period of tribulation and to Christ's visible return.

Within premillennialism, pretribulationists place the rapture before a seven-year tribulation, midtribulationists at its midpoint, prewrath advocates partway through the second half before God's wrath is poured out, and posttribulationists at the end, as part of the single visible return. Amillennialists, postmillennialists and preterists generally see no separate rapture at all: 1 Thessalonians 4 describes the one second coming.

A related historical question is whether a pretribulation rapture was taught before John Nelson Darby in the 1830s. Several earlier texts have been proposed, and each is debated.

positions.name: Pretribulation Rapture
positions.summary:
Pretribulationism teaches that Christ will come for his church before the seven-year tribulation (Daniel's seventieth week), raising dead believers and transforming living ones and taking them to heaven. After the tribulation, during which God deals especially with Israel and judges the world, Christ returns visibly with his saints to establish the millennial kingdom. The second coming therefore has two phases: the rapture (Christ for his saints, in the air) and the revelation (Christ with his saints, to the earth).

The view rests on the distinction between Israel and the church, on the conviction that the tribulation is entirely a period of divine wrath from which the church is exempt, and on the imminence of Christ's coming, meaning that no prophesied event must occur before the rapture. It is closely associated with dispensational premillennialism.

figures.name: John Nelson Darby
figures.profession: Brethren teacher and theologian
figures.bio: Darby developed and spread the doctrine of a rapture before the tribulation as part of his distinction between the heavenly church and earthly Israel. Pretribulationists generally regard him as having recovered or systematized a biblical teaching; critics regard him as its originator. Whether earlier writers held it is debated.

figures.bio: Walvoord gave the pretribulation view a thorough theological defense, listing arguments from the nature of the church, the purpose of the tribulation, and imminence.

figures.name: Hal Lindsey
figures.profession: Evangelist and author
figures.bio: A Dallas Seminary graduate who worked with Campus Crusade, Lindsey wrote a bestselling book connecting pretribulation teaching with Cold War and Middle Eastern events. It sold many millions of copies and shaped popular expectation in the 1970s.

positions.context:
Pretribulationism emerged among the Brethren in the 1830s within a revival of premillennial expectation in Britain. It spread to North America through Bible conferences, the Scofield Reference Bible and Bible institutes, becoming the most common view among American evangelicals and many Pentecostals in the twentieth century. It gained a vast popular audience through Hal Lindsey and the Left Behind novels and films.

The question of whether it was taught before Darby is contested: proponents point to Pseudo-Ephraem, Morgan Edwards and others; critics argue these sources are ambiguous, and some (notably Dave MacPherson) argued that it arose from Margaret MacDonald's 1830 vision, a claim most historians regard as unproven.
claims: The church will be raptured before the seven-year tribulation begins.
The tribulation is a period of divine wrath, from which the church has been promised deliverance.
Christ's coming for the church is imminent: no prophesied sign must precede it.
The rapture and the visible return are two distinct phases separated by at least seven years.
The tribulation concerns God's dealings with Israel and the unbelieving world, not the church.
The restrainer of 2 Thess 2 is the Holy Spirit working through the church, removed at the rapture.

scriptures.reading: The rapture: Christ descends to the air and believers are caught up, with no mention of judgment or of descending to earth.
Jesus delivers us from the wrath to come.
God has not destined believers for wrath.
The faithful church is kept out of the hour of trial coming on the whole world.
Christ will take his people to the Father's house, implying they go to heaven rather than straight back to earth.
The restrainer must be taken out of the way before the lawless one is revealed.
Believers wait for the blessed hope, an imminent event rather than the end of seven years of tribulation.
After the letters to the churches, the word church does not appear on earth until chapter 22, suggesting the church is in heaven during the judgments.
The seventieth week concerns your people (Israel), so the church is absent from it.

arguments.text: The church is repeatedly promised deliverance from coming wrath, and the seal, trumpet and bowl judgments are described as the wrath of the Lamb.
Believers are urged to watch and be ready because the Lord could come at any time; a posttribulational coming would be preceded by clear signs, making the warnings less meaningful.
If all believers are raptured and glorified at the end of the tribulation, there would be no mortal believers left to enter and populate the millennium.
Rapture passages and second coming passages differ in their details: the first describes meeting in the air and comfort, the second judgment and descent to the Mount of Olives.
The church is absent from the descriptions of the tribulation in Rev 6-18, where the focus shifts to Israel (the 144,000) and the nations.
Although debated, sources such as Pseudo-Ephraem and Morgan Edwards suggest that a removal of saints before tribulation was not entirely unknown before Darby.

critiques.text: Not all of the seventieth week is wrath; the first half consists of human wickedness and preliminary judgments, so the church need not be removed until the midpoint.

The great tribulation is the persecution of the saints by antichrist, not God's wrath; Scripture locates wrath after the cosmic signs, so a pretribulation rapture is not required to keep believers from wrath.
No passage clearly teaches two comings separated by seven years; the gathering of the elect follows the tribulation, and the church has always been promised tribulation in this world.

The view depends on a system (the Israel-church distinction and a future seventieth week) that is not evident in the texts, and it was unknown to the church's mainstream teachers for eighteen centuries.

responses.text: Revelation shows the Lamb opening the first seal; all seven seals belong to the same series of divine judgments, so wrath begins with the week itself.
The persecution by antichrist occurs within a period that God's judgments define as wrath; the cry of Rev 6:16-17 says the wrath has come, looking back over the seals.
The New Testament distinguishes a coming in the air from a coming to the earth, and the church's tribulation in this age is different from the unique eschatological tribulation.
The truth of a doctrine is established from Scripture, not from its date of articulation; many doctrines were clarified later in church history. Moreover, some early writers expressed imminence.

strawMen.strawMan: The pretribulation rapture was invented by Margaret MacDonald's vision.
strawMen.correction: This claim, popularized by Dave MacPherson, is disputed by most historians; MacDonald's account does not clearly describe a pretribulation rapture, and Darby gave exegetical reasons for his view.

strawMen.strawMan: Pretribulationists believe Christians will never suffer persecution.
strawMen.correction: They affirm that Christians suffer tribulation throughout the age; they deny only that the church will pass through the specific eschatological seventieth week.

strawMen.strawMan: Pretribulationism teaches escapism and indifference to the world.
strawMen.correction: Its proponents emphasize evangelism and holy living in light of an imminent return, though critics argue some popular forms encouraged disengagement.

positive: Encourages a lively expectation of Christ's return at any moment.
Motivated evangelism and missionary urgency.
Offers comfort that believers will not face God's wrath.
negative: Some fear it leaves believers unprepared for persecution.
Popular forms encouraged date-setting and sensationalism.
Critics argue it fostered cultural disengagement among some evangelicals.

adherents: Many Baptist, Bible church and Pentecostal congregations

positions.name: Midtribulation (Mid-Seventieth-Week) Rapture
positions.summary:
Midtribulationism holds that the church will be raptured at the midpoint of Daniel's seventieth week, three and a half years into the seven-year period. The first half contains the rise of antichrist and preliminary troubles caused largely by human wickedness, through which the church passes; the second half is the great tribulation and the outpouring of God's wrath, from which the church is removed.

Its best-known defender, Gleason Archer, called his view a mid-seventieth-week rapture to stress that the church is spared the wrath of the final three and a half years. Midtribulationists often identify the last trumpet of 1 Cor 15:52 with the seventh trumpet of Rev 11:15 and see the ascension of the two witnesses in Rev 11:11-12 as a picture of the rapture.

figures.profession: Old Testament scholar at Trinity Evangelical Divinity School
figures.bio: Archer was a respected evangelical Old Testament scholar and linguist. In a 1984 multi-view volume he defended a mid-seventieth-week rapture, arguing that the church is promised exemption from God's wrath but not from the persecution of the first half of the week.

positions.context: Midtribulationism appeared in the first half of the twentieth century as some premillennialists found pretribulational arguments unpersuasive but still believed the church would be spared the most intense judgments. It gained academic visibility through Buswell and Archer. It has always been a minority position, and from 1990 many who might have held it adopted the prewrath view, which shares its concern to distinguish tribulation from wrath.
claims: The seventieth week of Daniel is a future seven-year period divided into two halves of three and a half years.
The church will experience the first half of the week, including the rise of antichrist.
The church will be raptured at the midpoint, before the great tribulation and the outpouring of God's wrath.
The last trumpet of Paul corresponds to the seventh trumpet of Revelation.
The rapture and the visible return are distinct, separated by about three and a half years.
Scripture's repeated three-and-a-half-year periods mark the second half as the time of wrath.

scriptures.reading: The last trumpet is identified with the seventh and last trumpet of Revelation.
The two witnesses are called up in a cloud just before the seventh trumpet, picturing the rapture at the midpoint.
The saints are given into the little horn's hand for a time, times and half a time, the final three and a half years.
The covenant is broken in the middle of the week, marking a decisive shift.
The final period of intense trouble lasts three and a half years.
The abomination of desolation in the middle of the week inaugurates the great tribulation.
Believers are not destined for wrath, which falls in the second half.
The woman is protected for 1,260 days, the second half of the week.
The beast exercises authority for forty-two months.

arguments.text: Daniel and Revelation repeatedly single out a final three-and-a-half-year period (time, times and half a time; 42 months; 1,260 days) as the time of the most intense trouble.
Paul's last trumpet naturally matches the last trumpet in the series of seven in Revelation.
The view harmonizes the promise of exemption from wrath with the expectation that believers will witness the rise of antichrist.
Jesus marks the abomination of desolation as the trigger for flight and great tribulation, suggesting a turning point in the week.
The ascension of the two witnesses in a cloud before the seventh trumpet gives a narrative picture of a rapture at that point.

critiques.text: The whole seventieth week is wrath, beginning with the seals opened by the Lamb; and the midtribulation view destroys imminence, because the rapture can be dated three and a half years after a visible covenant.

The seventh trumpet is part of God's wrath, not the trigger for the gathering; and the great tribulation of Matt 24 is persecution by antichrist in the second half, during which the church is still present until it is cut short.

The last trumpet of Paul is the trumpet at the end of the age; equating it with the seventh trumpet of a separate book written decades later is speculative, and Matt 24 places the gathering after the tribulation.
Rev 11 is part of a symbolic vision; reading the witnesses' ascension as the church's rapture imposes a chronology on apocalyptic imagery.

responses.text: Imminence can mean the coming is the next major event for the church's hope, not that no event precedes it; the first seals describe human-caused troubles like war and famine.
The seventh trumpet announces the kingdom and the time for rewarding the saints, which fits the rapture and resurrection of believers.
Paul's readers knew trumpet imagery from Jewish eschatology; John's revelation clarifies which trumpet is last. Matt 24:31 may describe the gathering of Israel's remnant.
Symbolic visions still have referents; the witnesses' resurrection and ascension clearly echo resurrection and rapture language.

strawMen.strawMan: Midtribulationists believe Christians will be raptured exactly 1,260 days after a known date and can set a date.
strawMen.correction: They place the rapture at the midpoint of the week, but generally avoid date-setting and allow uncertainty about how the week begins.

strawMen.strawMan: Midtribulationism is a compromise with no exegetical basis.
strawMen.correction: It rests on specific arguments from the structure of the week and the trumpet sequence, defended by serious scholars such as Archer.

positive: Encourages believers to prepare for persecution while hoping for deliverance from wrath.
Draws attention to the structure of Daniel's seventieth week.
negative: Has remained a small minority view with limited institutional support.
Its identification of the last trumpet is widely regarded as weak, even by other premillennialists.

adherents: Many former midtribulationists now hold the prewrath view

positions.name: Prewrath Rapture
positions.summary:
The prewrath view holds that the church will go through the first part of Daniel's seventieth week, including the great tribulation, the persecution of believers by antichrist that begins at the midpoint. That persecution will be cut short by the coming of Christ, announced by cosmic signs in the sun, moon and stars. At that coming the church is raptured, and immediately afterward God's wrath, the day of the Lord, is poured out on the world through the trumpet and bowl judgments, before Christ's final victory at the end of the week.

The key distinction is between the wrath of Satan and antichrist against the saints, which believers may endure, and the wrath of God, from which believers are promised deliverance. Prewrath advocates usually place the rapture at the sixth seal of Revelation, before the seventh seal opens the trumpet judgments.

positions.context: The prewrath view emerged in the late 1980s among dispensationalists who became convinced that the church will face antichrist but who retained a future seventieth week and a distinction between rapture and final return. Rosenthal's 1990 book provoked responses from pretribulational scholars. The view has since gained a steady following, especially through online ministries, and academic recognition through Hultberg.
claims: The church will be present during the first part of the seventieth week and the great tribulation.
The great tribulation is antichrist's persecution of God's people, not God's wrath.
The great tribulation will be cut short by Christ's coming, signaled by cosmic disturbances.
The rapture occurs at Christ's coming before the day of the Lord's wrath begins.
The day of the Lord's wrath, beginning at the seventh seal, is poured out in the trumpet and bowl judgments.
Christ's parousia is a single, extended coming that begins with the rapture and includes wrath and the final descent.

scriptures.reading: Those days will be cut short for the sake of the elect, implying the elect are present during the great tribulation.
Immediately after the tribulation of those days, cosmic signs appear and the elect are gathered: this is the rapture.
Cosmic signs come before the great and dreadful day of the Lord.
The sixth seal's cosmic signs mark the arrival of the day of God's wrath.
A great multitude appears suddenly in heaven out of the great tribulation, picturing the raptured church.
The coming and our gathering will not take place until the apostasy and the man of lawlessness are revealed.
The day of the Lord comes as a thief on unbelievers, but believers are not destined for wrath.
As with Noah and Lot, deliverance of the righteous comes on the same day as the judgment begins.
The seventh seal opens the trumpet judgments, the beginning of God's wrath.

arguments.text: Jesus, Joel and Revelation all place cosmic signs before the day of the Lord; in Matthew the gathering follows these signs, so the rapture occurs just before wrath.
Revelation explicitly says the great day of wrath has come only at the sixth seal, so the earlier seals are not God's wrath.
Jesus' analogies of Noah and Lot show deliverance and judgment happening on the same day, matching a rapture that immediately precedes wrath.
The view keeps the promise of deliverance from wrath while honoring Paul's explicit statement that believers will see the man of lawlessness first.
The great multitude of Rev 7 appears in heaven between the sixth and seventh seals, having come out of the great tribulation.
The elect for whom the days are shortened are the same people Jesus addresses throughout the discourse, his disciples, representing the church.

critiques.text: All seven seals are opened by the Lamb and form one series of divine judgments; the cry of Rev 6:17 shows wrath already present in the seals. The view also denies imminence.
The prewrath scheme places the rapture at an undefined point in the second half, while Scripture marks the midpoint and the last trumpet as the decisive moments.
Matt 24:29 places the gathering after the tribulation of those days, and the coming of Rev 19 is the only visible return described; there is no clear text for a gap between rapture and final descent.
The view builds an elaborate timetable from apocalyptic visions that most of the church has read as parallel, symbolic portrayals of one final judgment.

responses.text: Opening the seals does not make their contents God's wrath any more than allowing persecution makes it God's wrath; the fifth seal shows martyrs crying for vengeance, which wrath has not yet answered.
The midpoint begins antichrist's persecution, not God's wrath; Jesus says those days are cut short, so the rapture occurs before the end of the week but after the midpoint.
After the tribulation fits prewrath, which places the rapture after the great tribulation is cut short; the day of the Lord then follows as a distinct period of wrath before the final battle.
Some recapitulation is granted, but the seals, trumpets and bowls show narrative progression (the seventh seal contains the trumpets), and the cosmic signs anchor the sequence.

strawMen.strawMan: The prewrath view is simply midtribulationism under a new name.
strawMen.correction: It places the rapture after the midpoint, at the cutting short of the great tribulation, and defines wrath differently from midtribulationism.

strawMen.strawMan: Prewrath advocates believe Christians must earn escape by enduring persecution.
strawMen.correction: They teach deliverance by grace; the church's presence in the great tribulation is a matter of chronology, not merit.

Engages closely with the text of the Olivet Discourse and Revelation.
Keeps a clear distinction between suffering and divine wrath.
negative: Caused divisions within dispensational ministries in the 1990s.
Its detailed timetable invites speculation about sequences of events.
Has limited acceptance in academic and denominational settings.

positions.name: Posttribulation Rapture
positions.summary:
Posttribulationism holds that the rapture and the second coming are a single event occurring after the tribulation. The church will be present through the final period of distress and the career of antichrist, preserved by God through it, and at Christ's visible return believers who have died will be raised and living believers transformed and caught up to meet him in the air, accompanying him as he comes to earth to reign.

Posttribulationists are premillennial; they expect Christ's earthly reign to follow his return. They stress that the church has always been called to endure tribulation, that the New Testament uses the same terms for Christ's coming in rapture and return passages, and that believers are protected from God's wrath without being removed from the world.

figures.name: Samuel Prideaux Tregelles
figures.profession: English biblical scholar and textual critic
figures.bio: Tregelles, an early associate of the Brethren and a major textual critic of the Greek New Testament, rejected the secret pretribulation rapture as it developed in the 1830s and argued that the church awaits one visible coming after antichrist.

works.author: Samuel Prideaux Tregelles
works.title: The Hope of Christ's Second Coming

figures.name: Alexander Reese
figures.profession: British Bible teacher and author
figures.bio: Reese wrote a lengthy, detailed rebuttal of the pretribulation teaching of Darby, Kelly and Scofield, which became a standard resource for later posttribulationists.

figures.name: George Eldon Ladd
figures.profession: New Testament scholar at Fuller Theological Seminary
figures.bio: Ladd's study of the vocabulary of the second coming argued that Scripture knows one blessed hope, the glorious appearing of Christ after the tribulation, and influenced many evangelicals away from pretribulationism.

figures.name: Robert H. Gundry
figures.profession: New Testament scholar at Westmont College
figures.bio: Gundry wrote a detailed exegetical defense of posttribulationism from within a broadly dispensational framework, examining every key text and the history of the pretribulation view.

positions.context: Before the nineteenth century, premillennial writers from Irenaeus onward generally assumed the church would face antichrist before Christ's coming. As a distinct position named in contrast to pretribulationism, posttribulationism was articulated by Tregelles and others who opposed Darby's teaching. In the twentieth century, Reese, Ladd and Gundry made it the leading alternative among premillennial scholars, and Douglas Moo represented it in the Three Views on the Rapture volumes.
claims: The rapture of the church occurs at the single, visible second coming of Christ.
The church will be present during the tribulation and the reign of antichrist.
God protects his people through tribulation rather than removing them from it.
Believers are exempt from God's wrath, which is distinct from tribulation.
The New Testament uses the same terms (parousia, apokalypsis, epiphaneia) for the coming that gathers the church and the coming in glory.
Meeting the Lord in the air means going out to welcome him and returning with him to earth.

scriptures.reading: The gathering of the elect with a loud trumpet follows the tribulation.
The trumpet, the archangel and the coming in clouds match the visible return; the meeting (apantesis) is a going out to escort the arriving King.
Our gathering to him will not occur until the apostasy and the man of lawlessness appear.
Believers receive relief when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven in flaming fire to judge, a single event bringing rest and judgment together.
The last trumpet raises the dead and defeats death, connected with the end of the age.
Jesus prays that the Father keep them from the evil one, not take them out of the world, using the same construction as Rev 3:10.
The first resurrection includes those who did not worship the beast, implying believers were present during antichrist's reign and are raised after it.
Wheat and weeds grow together until the harvest at the end of the age.
Believers go out to meet (apantesis) Paul and escort him back to Rome, illustrating the term's usage.

arguments.text: No passage explicitly teaches a rapture before the tribulation, while Matthew and 2 Thessalonians explicitly place the gathering after the tribulation or after antichrist appears.
The terms for the coming that believers await (parousia, apokalypsis, epiphaneia) are the same terms used for the coming in glory, suggesting one event.
Scripture consistently presents tribulation as the church's lot and God's protection as preservation through it, as with Israel in Egypt during the plagues.
The early church writers expected to face antichrist; none clearly teaches a pretribulation rapture, and the separate rapture became widespread only after the 1830s.
The meeting imagery in Paul reflects a known custom of a city's residents going out to meet an arriving dignitary and escorting him in, implying believers return with Christ to earth.
Revelation's saints are present during the beast's reign and are raised in the first resurrection after it.

critiques.text: Posttribulationism destroys imminence, makes the rapture pointless if believers immediately return, and leaves no mortal believers to populate the millennium.
It overlooks the promise of exemption from the wrath of the second half and the significance of the last trumpet at the midpoint.
It conflates the great tribulation with the day of the Lord's wrath and cannot explain where the church is during the trumpets and bowls.
Posttribulationism is right about the single coming but unnecessarily attaches it to a future seven-year tribulation and an earthly millennium.

responses.text: Imminence means the coming could be near and calls for constant readiness, not that no event may precede it; the meeting purpose is to escort the King. Converted Israel and spared nations may populate the millennium.
Paul's last trumpet is the final eschatological trumpet; Revelation's seventh trumpet belongs to a different series of judgments.
God's wrath falls on the wicked while his people are sealed and protected, as Israel was in Goshen during the plagues.
The disagreement concerns the millennium, a separate question; on the timing of the gathering, posttribulationists and the single-return view agree.

strawMen.strawMan: Posttribulationists believe Christians will suffer God's wrath.
strawMen.correction: They distinguish tribulation from wrath and hold that believers are protected from God's wrath while living through the tribulation.

strawMen.strawMan: In posttribulationism the rapture is a meaningless yo-yo trip up and down.
strawMen.correction: The meeting reflects the ancient custom of welcoming a king; believers are raised, glorified and join Christ's triumphal procession.

positive: Prepares believers for suffering and perseverance.
Grounds hope in a single, public, glorious appearing of Christ.
Resonates with persecuted churches around the world.
negative: Can produce anxiety about facing antichrist.
Has sometimes been associated with survivalist movements in popular culture.
Leaves some questions about the population of the millennium.

positions.name: No Separate Rapture (Single Return)
positions.summary:
Most Christians in history, including Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and most other Protestant traditions, have read 1 Thess 4:13-18 not as a separate rapture event but as a description of the one second coming of Christ at the end of history. When Christ returns visibly, the dead are raised, living believers are transformed and gathered to him, and the general resurrection and final judgment follow, leading to the new heavens and new earth.

This view is held by amillennialists, postmillennialists and partial preterists, who do not expect a future seven-year tribulation followed by an earthly millennium. It shares with posttribulationism the conviction that believers are gathered at the single visible return, but differs in seeing no subsequent earthly kingdom. Full preterists also deny a separate rapture but place the coming in AD 70.

figures.name: Augustine of Hippo
figures.profession: Bishop and theologian
figures.bio: Augustine's City of God treats Christ's coming, the resurrection and the last judgment as the climax of history, establishing the framework within which Western Christians read Paul's description of the Lord's descent.

figures.name: John Calvin
figures.profession: Reformer in Geneva
figures.bio: Calvin's commentaries read Paul's teaching on the Lord's descent as the final coming and resurrection, with no hint of a two-stage return.

works.author: John Calvin
works.title: Commentary on the Epistles to the Thessalonians

figures.name: Anthony A. Hoekema
figures.profession: Reformed theologian at Calvin Theological Seminary
figures.bio: Hoekema explained the single-return reading in detail and critiqued the pretribulation rapture as lacking clear biblical support.

figures.name: N. T. Wright
figures.profession: Anglican bishop and New Testament scholar
figures.bio: Wright argues that Paul's imagery in 1 Thess 4 draws on the custom of citizens going out to greet an arriving ruler and on Sinai and Daniel imagery, and that it describes Christ's royal arrival to renew creation, not the removal of believers from earth.

positions.context: For most of church history the question of a separate rapture did not arise; the creeds confessed that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead. When the pretribulation rapture spread in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, theologians of the historic confessional traditions responded by explaining why they read the relevant passages as a single return. In recent decades, New Testament scholarship on Greco-Roman parousia and apantesis customs has given the single-return reading fresh support.
claims: Christ's second coming is a single, visible, glorious event at the end of history.
1 Thess 4 describes the resurrection and gathering of believers at that one coming.
The resurrection of the righteous and the wicked and the final judgment occur together at the coming.
There is no future seven-year tribulation followed by an earthly millennium.
The church will experience tribulation throughout the age, possibly intensifying before the end.
Meeting the Lord in the air is a welcome of the returning King who comes to renew the earth.

scriptures.reading: A pastoral assurance that dead believers will not miss the Lord's coming; it describes the one coming in royal-visit language.
Relief for believers and judgment on persecutors happen together when the Lord is revealed from heaven.
All who are in the tombs come out at one hour, to life or to judgment.
When the Son of Man comes in glory, all nations are gathered and judged at once.
At the end of the age the righteous and wicked are separated in one harvest.
The day of the Lord brings the dissolution of the present order and the new heavens and new earth.
The resurrection and transformation at the last trumpet coincide with the final defeat of death.
Heaven receives Christ until the time of the restoration of all things, implying one return at the consummation.
One is taken and one left in the judgment that comes like the flood; this is the final coming, not a secret rapture.

arguments.text: Every New Testament passage that describes Christ's coming links it with the resurrection, the judgment, or the end of the age, never with a multi-year interval.
1 Thess 4 is loud and public (a shout, the archangel's voice, God's trumpet), hardly a secret event.

The creeds and confessions of nearly every Christian tradition confess one future coming to judge the living and the dead, and no separate rapture appears in mainstream teaching before the nineteenth century.
The word apantesis was used for citizens going out to greet an arriving ruler and escort him into the city, implying believers welcome Christ as he comes to earth rather than leaving with him.
Paul's purpose in 1 Thess 4 is to comfort grieving believers about the dead, not to provide an end-times chronology; in 1 Thess 5 he turns to the day of the Lord as part of the same subject.
In Jesus' teaching, those taken in judgment are like those swept away in the flood, so being taken is not a rapture of the righteous.

critiques.text: The single-return view rests on an amillennial or postmillennial framework that spiritualizes prophecy, and it cannot explain the differences between rapture passages (meeting in the air) and return passages (descent to the Mount of Olives).
It overlooks the detailed structure of the seventieth week in Daniel and Revelation.
It ignores the distinct period of the day of the Lord's wrath between the cosmic signs and the final battle.
It correctly unites rapture and return but neglects Rev 20's picture of a reign after the return and the first resurrection.

responses.text: The differences are differences of emphasis within one event; Zech 14 is prophetic imagery fulfilled in Christ's single coming, and both passages describe Christ coming with his holy ones.
Daniel's seventy weeks are fulfilled in Christ's first coming and the events that followed; Revelation's time periods are symbolic of the church age.
The day of the Lord in the New Testament arrives suddenly and brings final judgment and the new creation at once.
Rev 20 is read as a symbolic vision of the present age; the rest of the New Testament teaches a single general resurrection.

strawMen.strawMan: Those who deny a separate rapture do not believe Christians will be caught up to meet the Lord.
strawMen.correction: They affirm that living believers will be caught up to meet Christ, exactly as Paul says; they deny only that this is separated in time from the visible return.

strawMen.strawMan: Rejecting the rapture means rejecting the second coming.
strawMen.correction: This view strongly affirms a personal, bodily, visible second coming; it simply sees one coming rather than two stages.

positive: Maintains continuity with the creeds and the majority of church history.
Focuses Christian hope on resurrection and new creation.
Discourages speculative timetables.
negative: Can make the return of Christ seem distant and abstract in popular piety.
Some critics argue it underplays the distinctive details of prophecy.

readings.reading: Describes the rapture, a coming of Christ for his saints in the air, distinct from his later coming with his saints to the earth. Nothing in the passage mentions tribulation signs or judgment.
The rapture at the last trumpet, which midtribulationists connect with the seventh trumpet of Rev 11 at the middle of the seventieth week.
The rapture occurs at Christ's parousia after the great tribulation is cut short, when cosmic signs announce the day of the Lord, but before God's wrath falls.

The word meet (apantesis) describes citizens going out to welcome a visiting dignitary and escort him back; believers meet Christ in the air and return with him to earth at the one return after the tribulation.
This is the second coming itself, described with royal visitation imagery. Believers rise to greet the returning King, followed immediately by the general resurrection and judgment.
Kept from (tereo ek) the hour of trial means removed from the time period itself, not merely protected through it.
Promises protection from the hour of God's wrath, which midtribulationists see as the second half of the seventieth week.
The hour of trial is God's wrath in the day of the Lord, from which believers are kept by the rapture that precedes it.
The same phrase in John 17:15 means protection while remaining in the world; believers are preserved through the trial, not removed beforehand.
A promise to the first-century church in Philadelphia of protection during coming trial, with application to faithful believers in every age.
God has not destined us for wrath; since the whole tribulation is the outpouring of wrath, the church must be removed beforehand.
Wrath begins at the midpoint of the week, so the church is removed then.
Wrath is not the whole seventieth week; it is the day of the Lord that begins after the great tribulation is cut short.
Wrath here is final eschatological judgment (contrasted with salvation), not a period of tribulation; believers can suffer tribulation while being spared wrath.
The contrast is between final condemnation and salvation at the one day of the Lord, not a chronological scheme.
The elect gathered after the tribulation are tribulation saints and Israel, not the church, which was raptured earlier. The discourse addresses Jewish disciples about Israel's future.
The final visible return after the tribulation; the church was raptured earlier at the midpoint.
Immediately after the tribulation of those days (cut short), cosmic signs appear and angels gather the elect: this is the rapture before the day of the Lord's wrath.
The clearest text on timing: the gathering of the elect with a trumpet occurs after the tribulation, matching Paul's trumpet and gathering language.
Read either as Christ's final coming or, by preterists, as the judgment of AD 70 and the gospel's ingathering; in neither case is there a separate rapture.
The Thessalonians feared they were already in the day of the Lord; Paul reassures them it cannot have come because the restrainer (the Spirit through the church) has not been removed.
The apostasy and the revealing of the man of lawlessness at the temple occur at the middle of the week, followed by the gathering.
The coming and our gathering will not happen until the man of lawlessness is revealed, so believers will see antichrist before the rapture.
Our being gathered to him follows the apostasy and the revelation of the man of lawlessness, so the church is present for antichrist's career.
The coming and gathering are the single return, preceded by a final rebellion and lawless figure (or, for preterists, first-century events).
The mystery of the rapture: a sudden, signless transformation, distinct from the visible return.
The last trumpet corresponds to the seventh trumpet of Rev 11:15, sounded at the middle of the seventieth week.
The trumpet of the gathering after the cosmic signs; distinct from the judgment trumpets of Revelation.
The last trumpet is the final trumpet of the age, linked with the trumpet of Matt 24:31 after the tribulation.
The resurrection and transformation of believers at the one coming of Christ at the end of history.
Christ will come and take believers to the Father's house in heaven, implying a removal to heaven rather than an immediate return to earth.
A promise of the rapture that takes the church to heaven before the wrath of the second half.
A promise of being received by Christ, fulfilled at the prewrath rapture.
The passage does not say when or that believers stay in heaven for a period; it promises being with Christ, consistent with the single return.
A promise of eternal communion with Christ, often read in light of John's dwelling theme (John 14:23) rather than a chronology.
The sixth seal belongs to the tribulation judgments after the church has been raptured (Rev 4:1).
The seals belong largely to the first half of the week, before the wrath of the trumpets and bowls.
The sixth seal's cosmic signs mark the transition: the great day of their wrath has come, and the great multitude appears in heaven in Rev 7 immediately after.
The sixth seal reaches the end of the age and the coming of the Lamb's wrath at his single return.
One of Revelation's recapitulating portrayals of the final day of judgment.

timeline.title: Irenaeus expects the church to face antichrist
timeline.note: Against Heresies Book 5 (chapters 25-30) describes the church enduring antichrist's tribulation before Christ's coming, a view later cited by posttribulationists.

timeline.title: Augustine's single return
timeline.note: City of God Book 20 treats the coming, resurrection and judgment as one event at the end of the age.

timeline.title: Pseudo-Ephraem sermon on the last times
timeline.note: A Latin sermon attributed to Ephraem (dated variously from the fourth to seventh centuries) says the saints are gathered to the Lord before the tribulation so they will not see the confusion. Some pretribulationists read this as a pretribulation rapture; critics argue it refers to death or withdrawal rather than a rapture, and the text's date is uncertain.

timeline.title: Morgan Edwards' Two Academical Exercises
timeline.note: The American Baptist historian wrote (as a student essay, printed 1788) that saints would be caught up about three and a half years before the millennium. Some see an early pretribulation (or midtribulation) rapture; others note differences from later pretribulationism.

timeline.title: Margaret MacDonald's vision
timeline.note: A young Scottish woman in Port Glasgow described a prophetic vision of Christ's coming. Dave MacPherson argued it was the source of the pretribulation rapture; most historians, including some critics of pretribulationism, read her account as posttribulational in substance.

timeline.title: Powerscourt Conferences
timeline.note: Prophecy conferences in Ireland (1831-1833) where Darby and others discussed the rapture and the church's distinct calling.

timeline.title: Darby's pretribulation teaching
timeline.note: Darby taught a secret rapture before the tribulation by the early-to-mid 1830s; when he first held it (c. 1827 to 1833) is debated.

timeline.title: Tregelles opposes the secret rapture
timeline.note: Samuel Prideaux Tregelles, a former Brethren associate, publishes The Hope of Christ's Second Coming arguing for a single posttribulational return.

timeline.title: Scofield Reference Bible
timeline.note: Spreads pretribulationism among English-speaking evangelicals.

timeline.title: Alexander Reese's The Approaching Advent of Christ
timeline.note: A detailed posttribulational critique of Darby, Kelly and Scofield.

timeline.title: Ladd's The Blessed Hope
timeline.note: Ladd's case for posttribulationism becomes the standard evangelical alternative.

timeline.title: The Late Great Planet Earth
timeline.note: Hal Lindsey's bestseller popularizes pretribulationism for millions of readers.

timeline.title: Three Views on the Rapture
timeline.note: Paul Feinberg (pre), Gleason Archer (mid-seventieth week) and Douglas Moo (post) debate in one volume.

timeline.title: Rosenthal's The Pre-Wrath Rapture of the Church
timeline.note: Marvin Rosenthal, building on Robert Van Kampen's work, introduces the prewrath view.

timeline.title: Left Behind series begins
timeline.note: Tim LaHaye and Jerry Jenkins' novels bring pretribulation imagery into popular culture.

influence.note: Pretribulationism arose within premillennial circles that had earlier assumed the church would face antichrist, and defined itself against that view.
Midtribulationism retained the separation of rapture and return but moved the rapture to the middle of the week.
Prewrath kept the distinction between rapture and wrath but redefined when wrath begins.
Prewrath adopted the posttribulational point that the church faces antichrist's persecution.
Posttribulationism shares the classic single-return reading of 1 Thess 4 while adding a future millennium.

argumentMap.text: The church will be raptured before the tribulation begins.
The church is promised exemption from wrath, and the whole seventieth week is a time of divine wrath.
Imminence: believers are told to watch for Christ at any moment, which requires no prior signs.
Paul says the coming and our gathering will not occur until the apostasy and the man of lawlessness appear.
Paul addresses whether the day of the Lord has arrived, not the timing of the rapture; the restrainer's removal precedes antichrist's revelation.
Wrath and tribulation are distinct; the church suffers tribulation in every age but is spared final wrath.
The rapture happens at the midpoint of the seventieth week, at the last trumpet.
The seventh trumpet in Revelation is a judgment trumpet, not the gathering trumpet, and last may mean last in the age.
Rev 11:11-12 depicts witnesses called up into heaven in a cloud right before the seventh trumpet, a rapture image.
The rapture occurs after the great tribulation is cut short but before the day of the Lord's wrath.
The cosmic signs precede the day of the Lord (Joel), and in Revelation they come at the sixth seal, just before the great multitude appears in heaven.
Splitting the seventieth week into wrath and non-wrath portions is artificial; the seals are opened by the Lamb.
The rapture and second coming are a single event after the tribulation.
Paul and Jesus use the same features: trumpet, angels, clouds, gathering of the elect.
If the church is caught up and immediately returns, who populates the millennium in mortal bodies?
Surviving Jews converted at the return, or nations that did not take the mark, could enter the millennium in mortal bodies.
There is no separate rapture: 1 Thess 4 describes the one second coming at the end of history.
The coming is followed directly by the general resurrection, judgment and new creation, leaving no room for multiple stages.
Some texts describe Christ coming for his saints and others with his saints, suggesting two phases.
Both descriptions fit one event: the saints who have died come with him, and living saints meet him and escort him.
Historical question: a pretribulation rapture appears in sources before Darby.
Pseudo-Ephraem, Morgan Edwards and MacDonald texts are each ambiguous or differ substantially from Darby's system.
